titles.en: How is your NGO doing with technology?

intros.en: Ten quick questions, about three minutes. You will see where your organisation is doing well, where the gaps are, and which guides here will help most. Nothing is saved unless you choose to save it.

notes.en: This is a quick self-check, not an audit. It only knows what you tell it, and each area has just two questions — so treat it as a starting point for a conversation.

weakestOne.en: Your weakest area, and the guides here that help with it.

weakestMany.en: Your {count} weakest areas, and the guides here that help with them.

allGood.en: Nothing is scoring badly, so there is no single weak spot to point you at. The free programmes in this Hub are still worth a look — many go unclaimed simply because nobody applied.

unsureNote.en: You answered “I am not sure” {count} times. Those count as zero here, but they matter more than a plain no — if nobody knows who looks after something, that is the gap.

privacy.en: Your answers stay in this browser and are not sent anywhere.

summaries.en: Most of the basics are still ahead of you. That is a normal place to be, and the first steps are the cheapest ones: register for free software, get email with your own name on it, and turn on the phone code at login.
Some things are working and some are missing. The most useful work now is closing the gaps rather than adding new tools — especially anywhere you answered “not sure”.
The basics are mostly in place. From here the gains come from tidying up: one system instead of several, backups you have actually tested, and reports you can produce without starting over.
You are ahead of most organisations your size. The free programmes here are still worth checking — a lot go unclaimed simply because nobody applied.

descriptions.en: Whether you can claim the free and low-cost software your NGO is entitled to.

advice.en: Most free software programmes start with one check of your NGO's registration. Do it once and many of them open up.

prompts.en: Have you registered your NGO with TechSoup or Goodstack, so you can claim free software?
Do you keep your registration papers together, so applying is quick when you need to?

descriptions.en: The email and file tools your team uses every day.

advice.en: Email with your own name on it looks professional to funders. And files kept in the organisation's account do not walk out of the door when someone leaves.

prompts.en: Does your team use email addresses with your organisation's own name, instead of personal Gmail accounts?
Are shared files kept in the organisation's own account, so nothing is lost when someone leaves?

descriptions.en: Keeping accounts safe, and being able to get your files back.

advice.en: A code on your phone at login stops most break-ins and costs nothing. And a backup nobody has ever opened is only a hope.

prompts.en: When you log in, do your accounts ask for a code on your phone as well as a password?
Are your important files backed up automatically — and has anyone checked the backup really works?

descriptions.en: How funders, supporters and communities find you and hear from you.

advice.en: A funder will look you up before they reply to you. Make sure what they find is current.

prompts.en: If a funder opened your website today, would it show the work you are doing now?
Do you message supporters from an organisation account, rather than from staff members' own phones?

descriptions.en: Keeping your programme records in order, and getting reports out of them.

advice.en: If every report means rebuilding the numbers, the problem is where the data sits — not how hard your team works.

prompts.en: Is your programme data kept in one place your team shares, instead of many separate spreadsheets?
When a report is due, can you get the numbers out without redoing the work by hand?
